units.headline: One operator, dozens of apparent Kenyan supporters
units.summary: An unidentified Kenyan operator used Claude to produce batches of 50 posts posing as ordinary people's political opinions, according to Anthropic's September threat report. Some praised energy minister Opiyo Wandayi for halting a planned electricity-tariff increase. Others portrayed the opposition as divided. Anthropic found no evidence of government involvement and assessed the operation as having failed to reach or influence real users. The report covers activity disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026.
units.perspective: A campaign can impersonate a crowd by giving one message dozens of apparently independent voices. This operator used the same approach for commercial marketing. The intended deception lay in who appeared to be speaking, rather than in any new political argument.

units.headline: Prosecutors want to use a defendant's ChatGPT questions against him
units.summary: Christopher John Duff has pleaded not guilty to four restricted-data charges in New South Wales. Prosecutors allege he used AI to write a scraper and accessed 8,769 restricted court documents. At a hearing reported on 10 September, they said they intended to use his later ChatGPT questions about whether the access was illegal. His lawyer, Daniel McMahon, argues that asking afterwards whether the access was illegal does not prove Duff knew it was unauthorised when he accessed the documents. The hearing was adjourned; the report describes no final ruling on the conversations' admissibility.
units.perspective: Asking a chatbot for help after a legal problem may create a record for the opposing side. Prosecutors want to use Duff's questions as evidence of what he knew. The defence's response shows why a question's timing matters as much as its wording.

units.headline: Irish witnesses must declare that AI has not rewritten their evidence
units.summary: A generative-AI practice direction for Ireland's High Court took effect on 1 September. It does not ban AI-assisted legal drafting. Witness statements and affidavits, however, must open with a declaration that AI has not generated their substantive content, unless the court directs otherwise. The declaration covers rephrasing as well as strengthening, diluting or embellishing the account. Formatting and spelling checks are permitted. The court wants evidence to reflect the witness's personal recollection.
units.perspective: Polishing a witness's language can also polish away hesitation or change the strength of a recollection. The Irish rule treats that risk as part of the evidence problem, even when AI invents no event. In testimony, an awkward account may carry information that a smoother version loses.

units.headline: California sets rules for AI auditors, without requiring every system to be audited
units.summary: California signed two laws on 9 September governing AI auditors. SB813 calls for standards for designated independent verification organisations by January 2028, including competence and independence. The criteria must bar fees contingent on an assessment's result. The law expressly does not require AI developers or operators to obtain an audit. AB1405 requires a registry by January 2029 and, from then, bars unregistered providers from offering covered AI audits. Auditors must not review their own work. These are future requirements, not an audit system already operating.
units.perspective: An audit offers little reassurance if its author is paid for a favourable answer or is checking their own work. California is setting rules for the reviewers without requiring audits across the board. Credibility will depend on who checks a system, as well as what they check.

units.headline: A synthetic Bolsonaro endorsement falls outside Brazil's election-advertising ban
units.summary: At the Liberal Party's national convention on 25 July, an AI recreation of Jair Bolsonaro's image and voice endorsed his son Flávio's presidential candidacy. A rival federation sought the video's removal and a fine. On 1 September, Brazil's Superior Electoral Court rejected the fine by four votes to three. The majority treated the message as internal party communication without an explicit request for votes. Broadcasting the convention online did not automatically turn it into electoral advertising. In a separate five-to-two vote, the court defined deepfakes and held that the prohibition applies when the content qualifies as electoral advertising.
units.perspective: A synthetic endorsement can reach the public yet fall outside a ban on election deepfakes. Brazil's court treated this video as internal party communication. To enforce the ban, courts must classify the political message as well as identify the manipulated image.

units.headline: US court protects in-home possession of some synthetic abuse images
units.summary: On 25 August, a US appeals court upheld dismissal of a charge against Steven Anderegg for possessing obscene AI-generated depictions of child sexual abuse at home. Prosecutors conceded the images did not depict or link to an actual child. The appeal did not remove the separate production, distribution and transfer charges. Supreme Court precedents on private possession of obscenity and computer-generated images controlled the case, the Seventh Circuit held. Two judges asked for further Supreme Court guidance on AI. This was no general permission to create or circulate abuse imagery.
units.perspective: AI can make a fictional image look like the record of a real crime. The Supreme Court's child-protection rationale, however, centred on actual victims. The appeals judges could question how that boundary works with today's technology, but could not rewrite binding precedent themselves.

units.headline: Debian keeps the human contributor responsible for AI-written work
units.summary: Debian developers adopted a responsible-use policy for generative AI, announced on 30 August. AI-assisted contributions must meet the same standards of correctness, maintainability and legal compliance as other work. Contributors must understand, review and test their submissions, rather than upload them blindly. Disclosure of substantial AI assistance is encouraged, not mandatory. Automated mass bug reports or patches call for prior discussion and consensus. Contributors must not send non-public sensitive information to third-party models without explicit approval.
units.perspective: Generating a patch does not supply someone who can explain it, repair it or maintain it. Debian keeps that responsibility with the contributor and asks for agreement before automation creates work for the wider project. Its policy addresses the burden on recipients, not just the convenience of producing submissions.

units.headline: The FDA considers testing medical AI in clinics before its answers affect care
units.summary: On 18 August, the US Food and Drug Administration released a discussion paper asking how to assess generative-AI medical devices. It considers an approach inspired by the assessment of human clinicians: competency tests alongside evidence of clinical performance. The finished device would be evaluated in its intended configuration, not a foundation model by itself. One possible method is shadow deployment: the device processes real clinical inputs, but its outputs are recorded without being shown to clinicians or patients or affecting care. Comments are due by 19 October. The paper is exploratory, not guidance or a new regulatory requirement.
units.perspective: Good benchmark answers do not establish that a device will work well with patients, staff and a clinic's routines. Shadow deployment would let investigators compare its answers with actual decisions before anyone relies on them. It offers a way to learn from real use without first giving the tool a role in care.
